title: How Police Interrogation Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain police interrogation in the United States, from the historical third degree and the Brown v. Mississippi (1937) ruling, through the mid-century voluntariness rules, to John Reid's nine-step Reid Technique and its critics. They cover psychological tactics (good cop/bad cop, maximization, minimization, stopping denials, theme development), the debunked eye-movement lie-detection myth (Richard Wiseman's research), false confessions and notable exonerations (Peter Reilly, Earl Washington Jr., the Central Park Five), the Nicole Frederick Detroit case, the British PEACE model, and the Mr. Big technique. The episode closes with tips for suspects and a listener mail segment about Jittery Joe's Coffee.
topics: Miranda rights and right to counsel

segments.title: Opening banter and side reading
segments.summary: Hosts joke about their own run-ins with police, list related articles, and introduce police interrogation as a controversial subject in the police series.

segments.title: Third degree and coerced confessions history
segments.summary: Early US interrogations used physical abuse and deprivation, known as the third degree. Brown v. Mississippi (1937) led the Supreme Court to reject a coerced confession. By the 1950s, coerced confessions were ruled involuntary and signed confessions became standard.

segments.title: Psychological manipulation and classic interrogation tactics
segments.summary: Police replaced physical coercion with psychological manipulation, relying on stress and human tendencies. Tactics discussed include good cop bad cop, maximization, and minimization. John Reid, a polygraph examiner, developed the Reid Technique, which is widely used and criticized.

segments.title: Reid Technique criticism and police deception
segments.summary: The Reid Technique is defended by Reid but criticized as based on armchair psychology and presumption of guilt. Police may lie about evidence, and courts have upheld this. Studies suggest false confessions can follow from such deception, especially among vulnerable people.

segments.title: Interrogation room design and initial interview
segments.summary: The Reid manual describes a bare interrogation room with a one-way mirror and out-of-reach light switches to induce helplessness. The initial interview is meant to assess guilt or innocence and set a behavioral baseline through rapport-building.

segments.title: Eye movement lie detection myth
segments.summary: The popular belief that eye movements left or right reveal lying is debunked. Richard Wiseman's study of press conferences found no correlation with lying. Anxiety is also not a reliable sign of lying.

segments.title: Reid Technique steps: confrontation, theme development, denials
segments.summary: Steps of the Reid Technique include confrontation, reading nonverbal cues, theme development with a softer tone, and stopping denials. Objections are treated differently from denials and turned into justifications. The hosts discuss how a suspect who gives a lawyer-like or justified answer can be drawn in.

segments.title: Right to counsel, false confessions and exonerations
segments.summary: Suspects often fail to ask for a lawyer because interrogators discourage it. The hosts discuss false confession rates, the Innocence Project, and cases such as Peter Reilly, Earl Washington Jr., and the Central Park Five. Guilty suspects may remain free when innocent people are convicted.

segments.title: Nicole Frederick Detroit case and brainwashing parallels
segments.summary: The Nicole Michelle Frederick case in Detroit in 2003 is an example of the Reid method. Detective Victor Lauria used alternative themes until she confessed to shaking her two-year-old stepdaughter. The hosts compare the methods to brainwashing techniques.

segments.title: PEACE model and Mr. Big technique
segments.summary: Britain developed the PEACE model after false confessions came to light, focusing on information gathering and recorded interviews rather than accusation. The Mr. Big technique, used in Canada, involves an undercover officer building trust over months.

segments.title: Tips for suspects
segments.summary: Advice for people being interrogated: remain silent, ask for a lawyer, and avoid bonding with the interrogator. Invoking the right to counsel in the US should stop questioning.

segments.title: Listener mail: Jittery Joe's Coffee
segments.summary: A listener from Athens, Georgia, sends greetings from a honeymoon and describes a gift of Jittery Joe's Coffee.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts close with contact information and a plug for the website.
